-Solve the given spreadsheet manipulation question precisely:
-- Read the instruction, spreadsheet content preview, instruction type, and answer position carefully before writing any code.
-- For Cell-Level Manipulation questions, modify or fill in values ONLY within the exact cell(s) given in answer_position.
-- For Sheet-Level Manipulation questions, modify or fill in values ONLY within the cell range given in answer_position — never touch cells outside that range.

+Your output file is graded cell by cell against a reference answer. The grader re-opens the
+saved .xlsx and compares each cell in answer_position: numbers match when they agree to 2
+decimal places; a date/time matches only when it is a REAL date/time value (a text rendering
+of it does not match); any other text must match exactly. Only cells inside answer_position
+are graded, but changes you make OUTSIDE the intended edit can still corrupt the file. Write
+code whose output satisfies this grader.
+## Where to write
+- Modify ONLY the cell(s)/range given in answer_position. For Cell-Level, answer_position is
+  the exact cell(s). For Sheet-Level, it is the MAXIMUM range you may modify — within it,
+  change only what the instruction actually requires and leave every other cell at its
+  original value (do not fill cells the instruction does not ask you to change).
+- If answer_position has NO sheet name (no "!"), the target is the FIRST sheet of the
+  workbook — write there. If it names a sheet (e.g. 'INPUTS'!C15), write to that exact sheet.
+  Never write your answer to a different sheet than the one the grader will check.
+- Always save to the exact output_path, creating any missing parent directories first.
+## How to edit the file — avoid collateral damage
+- Prefer editing the workbook IN PLACE with openpyxl: `wb = openpyxl.load_workbook(path)`,
+  set only the target cells (`ws['A1'] = value` or `ws.cell(row, column).value = value`),
+  then `wb.save(output_path)`. This leaves all other cells, sheets, headers and formatting
+  untouched.
+- Do NOT round-trip an entire sheet through pandas (`pd.read_excel` then `df.to_excel`) when
+  the file has other cells, sheets, headers or formatting to preserve: `df.to_excel` rewrites
+  the whole sheet, turns blank header cells into `Unnamed: N`, and drops the other sheets. If
+  you must use pandas, read with `header=None` and write with
+  `df.to_excel(output_path, index=False, header=False)` so headers and blank cells survive.
+- Keep each cell's original data type. When a column holds ID/code values stored as text
+  (e.g. "0012", "70092-9054-05"), read it as text (`pd.read_excel(..., dtype=str)`) so the
+  values are not silently converted to numbers.
+## Produce values of the right kind
+- Compute and write LITERAL values, never live spreadsheet formulas — the grader reads cached
+  values and a formula written by openpyxl reads back as empty.
+- Write a number as a number. Write a date/time/datetime as a REAL `datetime.date` / `time` /
+  `datetime` value (or the Excel serial number) — NEVER a string built with
+  `strftime` / `str()` / Excel `TEXT()`, because a text rendering of a date or time does not
+  match the real value the grader expects.
+- When you replicate a spreadsheet sort, use a STABLE sort so rows that are equal on the sort
+  key keep their original relative order (`df.sort_values(..., kind='mergesort')`); Excel
+  sorts are stable, and an unstable sort reorders tied rows and fails.
+- When an instruction says to DELETE rows/data, remove those rows and shift the remaining rows
+  up so they stay contiguous — unless the instruction clearly means only to blank the cells.
+## Recover from mistakes
+- If execution raises an error, read the traceback and fix the code; never resubmit a code
+  block identical to one that already ran.
+- If a lookup, filter or aggregation leaves target cells empty/None/0 or drops nearly every
+  row, your key or assumption is wrong — re-derive it from the ACTUAL data (e.g. the real
+  min/max of a date column, or the real dropdown value), not from unrelated label cells, and
+  write again.
